p: Dillmann has "windows" in the fourth gate; the EOTC print has "gates."

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851)
Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church printed Bible (EOTC)

why: The windows beside the gates were introduced in 72:3, and 75:7 again speaks of windows giving off heat. A gate with twelve more gates inside it makes less sense, so "windows" is probably the older reading.

p: The EOTC print adds "because of its sign," as in 72:13 and 72:19.

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851)
Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church printed Bible (EOTC)
readings.orig: ሠላሳ ወአሐደ ጽባሐ በእንተ ትእምርተ ዚኣየ
readings.en: thirty-one mornings because of its sign
readings.plain: for thirty-one mornings, because of its sign,

why: The shorter text is followed, since a scribe is more likely to fill in a familiar phrase from 72:13 and 72:19 than to drop it. The meaning is the same: this is one of the four added days.

p: Both Ethiopic texts say the day is "seven" parts, which makes 19. Charles reads six.

readings.w: Charles's English (1917), correcting the number
Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851) and Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church printed Bible (EOTC)

why: Day and night always add up to 18 parts in this chapter, and midwinter must mirror midsummer (12 and 6, 72:14). Twelve plus seven is 19, so "seven" is an early copying error that both Ethiopic texts share. The Plain follows the number the scheme requires, as Charles did; no manuscript reading of "six" is reported here.

p: The EOTC print gives the day "one part," a slip for seven.

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851)
Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church printed Bible (EOTC)

why: Eleven parts of night and seven of day make 18, as the scheme requires. The EOTC's "one" cannot be right.

t: Thirteen and a half, or fourteen and a half?
p: Dillmann has "seven and seven" parts dark; the EOTC print has "seven and six."

readings.w: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church printed Bible (EOTC)
readings.orig: ሰብዐቱ ወስድስቱ እድ ወንፍቃ (säbʿätu wäsdəstu ʾəd)
readings.en: seven and six parts and a half

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851)
readings.en: seven and seven parts and a half

why: The moon has just received "half of one part" of light out of fourteen, so the dark part should be thirteen and a half. The EOTC's "seven and six" gives that; Dillmann's "seven and seven" (fourteen and a half) is more than the whole moon. The fractions in 73:5–8 are tangled in every text, so this choice is not certain.

p: Dillmann: the moon "changes" its settings. EOTC: it "completes" them.

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851)
Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church printed Bible (EOTC)

why: The next verses describe the moon setting in different gates in different months (74:5–8), which fits "changes." "Completes" may come from the many uses of that verb in 74:3.

p: The EOTC print and Dillmann's manuscripts have "which is called the sea" after "north"; Dillmann brackets the words as doubtful.

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851), leaving out the words he brackets as doubtful
EOTC printed Bible (unbracketed); Dillmann's bracketed words
readings.orig: ነፋሳት ዘመንገለ መስዕ ዘስሙ ባሕር (zäsmu baḥr)
readings.en: the winds toward the north, whose name is sea
readings.plain: the north winds, the quarter called the sea

why: The Plain drops words that the EOTC prints. Dillmann, who edited the text from several manuscripts, judged them doubtful and bracketed them. They also make no sense in context: the north is nowhere called "the sea" in the book. It holds seas (77:3), and that may be where a reader's note came from. Readers who prefer the EOTC can switch to that reading.

a: will not appear at the times set for them
p: Dillmann: the stars "will not appear" at their times. EOTC: they "will not turn."

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851)
readings.en: and they will not be seen
readings.plain: will not appear at the times set for them

readings.w: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church printed Bible (EOTC)
readings.plain: will not turn at the times set for them

why: "Not appear at its time" is the refrain of this poem (80:2; 80:4), so Dillmann's reading fits. The EOTC's verb repeats "change" from earlier in the verse.

t: Children of the world, or of Adam?
p: Dillmann: "the children of the world." EOTC: "the children of Adam," that is, humankind.

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851)
Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church printed Bible (EOTC)

why: Both mean all human beings. The Plain follows Dillmann; Charles has "the children of men." The EOTC print also has "the great Lord" (ዐቢይ, as Charles has) and adds "and I wept" (ወበከይኩ) before "over the children of Adam."

a: and no guilt found against him
p: The EOTC print adds "on the day of judgment."

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851)
readings.en: and no guilt was found against him
readings.plain: and no guilt found against him

readings.w: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church printed Bible (EOTC)
readings.en: and no guilt was found against him on the day of judgment
readings.plain: and no guilt found against him on the day of judgment

why: The shorter text is followed. The EOTC's phrase spells out what the blessing implies, and Charles's English ("no day of judgement shall be found") may show that some of his manuscripts also had "judgment" here.

p: Both Ethiopic texts here say "three"; Charles printed "seven."

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851) and Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church printed Bible (EOTC)
Ethiopic manuscripts followed by Charles, as reported in his edition (1912) and English (1917)

why: In the Animal Apocalypse three angels take Enoch up (see 87:3–4), which fits "three." "Seven" matches the seven holy angels of 20:1–8. The Plain follows the Ge'ez texts available here.

p: The names are spelled differently in Dillmann and the EOTC print.

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851)
Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church printed Bible (EOTC)

why: Angel names were copied by scribes who did not know their meaning, so spellings drift. The Plain follows Dillmann and uses the same spelling in 82:18.

a: All the days of his light
p: Dillmann: "the days of his light." EOTC: "the days of his rule," as in 82:15.

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851)
readings.plain: All the days of his light

readings.w: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church printed Bible (EOTC)
readings.plain: All the days of his rule

why: Dillmann's reading is the less expected one, and it suits a leader called "the Shining Sun"; the EOTC's "rule" matches the other seasons (82:15; 82:17; 82:20). Either way the season has 91 days.

a: the Most High will come down there
p: The Ge'ez says God "will come down" in the south. Milik reports that the Aramaic says the Great One "dwells" there.

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851) and EOTC printed Bible
readings.en: the Most High will come down there
readings.plain: the Most High will come down there

readings.w: Aramaic, Qumran Cave 4, 4Q209 (4QAstronomical Enoch b) fragment 23 with 4Q210, as read and restored by Milik (1976) and reported by Nickelsburg and VanderKam (2012); known here only from their report, not checked against the edition
readings.orig: (Aramaic not quoted here; reported sense: "there the Great One dwells," with dar "dwell" explaining darom "south")

why: The Plain translates the Ge'ez. The Aramaic is older, but the line is broken and partly restored, and its exact wording is known here only from Milik's report. If the report is right, "dwells" is the original and explains the name of the south by wordplay; the Ge'ez "will come down" may come from a misread or a deliberate change. Readers can switch to the reported Aramaic sense.
